claims.text: The target alloy is a quaternary equiatomic FCC alloy.
The target alloy has a homogeneous solid-solution microstructure without significant precipitates or secondary phases.
The target alloy has moderate-to-high stacking-fault energy.
Between 673 and 873 K, the target alloy's yield strength will be insensitive to strain rate from 0.001 to 0.1 s^-1, with m approximately zero.
The strain-rate-insensitive yield plateau is caused by a kinetic balance between dislocation accumulation or pile-up hardening and dynamic recovery.
Thermally generated super-jogs on edge dislocations act as barriers to slip.
Dislocation annihilation and rearrangement provide dynamic-recovery softening that offsets dislocation hardening.
Plastic yielding in the proposed regime remains dislocation-based rather than transformation-based.
Sufficiently high stacking-fault energy suppresses deformation-induced TRIP and amorphization.
Thermal activation permits rapid dislocation climb, thereby suppressing phase-transformation-mediated deformation.
Deformation-induced amorphization can be a competing mechanism in compositionally complex alloys under sufficiently severe deformation.
Tensile deformation can induce a crystal-structure phase transformation in a compositionally complex alloy.
If stacking-fault energy is too low, deformation may shift to twinning or an FCC-to-HCP transformation and eliminate the plateau.
Dynamic recrystallization at higher temperature would drastically reduce strength.
Ductility may decrease at higher strain rates because less time is available for dynamic recovery.
Conventional FCC alloys generally have positive strain-rate sensitivity because of thermally activated dislocation glide.
The temperature interval of the proposed plateau depends on the activation energy for dislocation climb.
Trace oxygen or other impurities may cause embrittlement or precipitate formation and alter the plateau.
A high-temperature strength plateau was observed in NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 between approximately 873 and 1073 K.
